title: Syllogisms
tagline: Year 2 — Drawing valid conclusions from All, No, Some and Some-not statements

introduction.overview: A syllogism gives two or more statements about classes of objects (All A are B, No A is B, Some A are B, Some A are not B) and asks which conclusions must follow. A conclusion follows only if it is true in every possible Venn-diagram arrangement of the statements, not merely in one. The reliable method is to draw all possible diagrams and test each conclusion against all of them.
introduction.placementRelevance: Syllogism questions are commonly asked in company reasoning rounds, usually with two statements and two or three conclusions.
introduction.realWorldContext: Deductive reasoning is the basis of logical arguments in law, programming conditions and database queries.

learningObjectives: Know the four statement types and their Venn pictures
Know the conversion rules between statements
Combine two statements to derive new conclusions
Test conclusions against every possible diagram

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A universal statement (All, No) talks about the whole class. A particular statement (Some, Some not) talks about part of it. Particular statements do not allow strong conclusions.

coreDefinitions: All A are B (A): the A circle lies inside the B circle (or equals it).
No A is B (E): the A and B circles are separate.
Some A are B (I): the circles overlap, at least partly.
Some A are not B (O): at least part of A lies outside B.
A conclusion "follows" if it is true in every diagram consistent with the statements.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: The statements describe a picture, but usually several pictures fit. A conclusion that is true in all of them is a valid deduction. A conclusion that is true in some and false in others is only a possibility, so it does not follow.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Draw the most general picture first (circles barely touching), then redraw with circles inside each other where the statements allow. Check each conclusion in every picture.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Conversion
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: No A is B ⇒ No B is A;  Some A are B ⇒ Some B are A;  All A are B ⇒ Some B are A
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: All cats are dogs ⇒ some dogs are cats

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: All + All
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: All A are B, All B are C ⇒ All A are C
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: All cats are dogs, all dogs are birds

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: All + No
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: All A are B, No B is C ⇒ No A is C
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: A is inside B, B is separate from C.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Some + All
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Some A are B, All B are C ⇒ Some A are C
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Some pens are books, all books are tables

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Either-or pair
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Some A are B and No A is B (and similar) are complementary
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: One of them must be true.
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Some B are not A / All B are A

mainNarrative: The four statement types give four pictures. All A are B: A inside B. No A is B: separate circles. Some A are B: overlapping circles. Some A are not B: part of A outside B. Remember that "Some" means at least one.

Two universal statements usually chain. All cats are dogs and all dogs are birds give all cats are birds, but not all birds are cats. A universal affirmative plus a universal negative gives a universal negative: all A are B and no B is C give no A is C.

A particular statement with a universal one gives a particular conclusion. Some pens are books and all books are tables give some pens are tables. Two particular statements (Some A are B, Some B are C) give no conclusion between A and C, because the overlaps may be in different parts of B.

To test a conclusion, draw all possible diagrams. If the conclusion fails in even one, it does not follow. If one of two conclusions must be true in every diagram (such as "Some B are not A" and "All B are A" when "All A are B" is given), then "either I or II follows".
For three statements, combine in pairs step by step, then test each conclusion against the combined picture.

deepDiveAspects.title: Existential import
deepDiveAspects.content: Aptitude tests usually assume the classes are non-empty, so "All A are B" implies "Some A are B". Follow the convention of the test.

deepDiveAspects.title: Possibility vs necessity
deepDiveAspects.content: The phrase "follows" means "must be true". A conclusion that could be true but need not be is rejected.

solvedExamples.title: All plus All
solvedExamples.question: Statements: All cats are dogs. All dogs are birds. Conclusions: I. All cats are birds. II. All birds are cats.

steps.title: Conclusion I
steps.explanation: C is inside B, so all cats are birds: follows.

steps.title: Conclusion II
steps.explanation: B is bigger than C, so not all birds are cats: does not follow.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: A smaller class is always inside the larger.

solvedExamples.title: Some plus All
solvedExamples.question: Statements: Some pens are books. All books are tables. Conclusions: I. Some pens are tables. II. All tables are books.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: The overlap with B lies inside T.

steps.title: Draw
steps.explanation: P overlaps B; B is inside T.

steps.title: Conclusion I
steps.explanation: The pens that are books are inside T: follows.

steps.title: Conclusion II
steps.explanation: T may be larger than B: does not follow.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The overlap region stays inside T.

solvedExamples.title: Either-or
solvedExamples.question: Statement: All A are B. Conclusions: I. Some B are not A. II. All B are A.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: In some diagrams A = B; in others A is smaller.

steps.title: Case 1
steps.explanation: A inside B with extra B: I is true, II false.

steps.title: Case 2
steps.explanation: A = B: I false, II true.

steps.title: Combine
steps.explanation: One of I or II is true in every case.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Draw the minimum and the maximum overlap pictures; a conclusion must hold in both. Use the combination table for All/No/Some.

commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Must be true in every diagram.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Eliminate conclusions with "All" or "No" that come from "Some" statements.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: The combination table solves most items.

summaryBullets: All + All, All + No, Some + All.

keyTakeaways: Must be true in every case.
selfCheckQuestions: Can I combine All and No?
Can I reject a possible-but-not-certain conclusion?
Can I spot an either-or pair?
